opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most practical questions right now. The way I see it, the two kinds of layers are good at fundamentally different things, so the question isn't really "which one wins" but "how do you split the work between them."

Linear layers, whether it's something like Mamba, gated linear attention, or the DeltaNet family, compress the entire history into a fixed-size state. That makes them very efficient: constant memory per token at inference and linear compute in training. They're great at local pattern modeling, at smoothly tracking state, and with the delta rule they're even decent at some associative recall. But because the state is fixed-size, there's an information bottleneck. When you need precise retrieval, like copying a long string or finding a needle in a long context, a fixed-size memory just can't hold everything losslessly.

Global softmax attention is the opposite. Its KV cache grows with the sequence, so it's expensive, but it can retrieve anything exactly. So in a hybrid, I think of the attention layers as a kind of precise "lookup" capability that you sprinkle in, and the linear layers do most of the heavy lifting of sequence mixing.

Empirically, what people have found, and what we've seen too, is that you don't need many attention layers. Ratios like one global attention layer for every three to seven linear layers seem to recover most of the retrieval performance of a full Transformer, sometimes even beat it, while getting a big chunk of the efficiency gains. Placement also matters somewhat. You generally don't want all the attention layers bunched at the beginning; spreading them through the depth, especially having some in the middle and later layers, tends to work better for retrieval.

Another point I'd make is that the stronger your linear layer, the fewer attention layers you need. If your linear layer is weak, like a plain linear attention without gating or the delta rule, the attention layers have to compensate for a lot. With something like Gated DeltaNet, the linear part already handles a lot of in-context recall, so you can push the ratio further toward linear.

And there's also the option of using sliding-window attention as a middle ground. Local attention is cheap and handles short-range precise interactions really well, which frees the linear layers to focus on longer-range state tracking. So a lot of designs end up as a three-way mix: linear layers, some sliding-window layers, and a small number of full global attention layers.

Ultimately the trade-off depends on your deployment target. If you care mostly about long-context inference cost, say for reasoning models generating very long chains of thought, you want to push the attention fraction down as far as quality allows, because the KV cache really becomes the bottleneck. If your workload is retrieval-heavy, you might keep a few more global layers. But I'm fairly convinced that the end state isn't pure Transformers or pure linear models. It's hybrids, and the interesting research is in making the linear part expressive enough that the attention part can be as small as possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that the trade-off isn't really "attention versus linear" as two competing ideas. They're good at different things, and a hybrid is just admitting that honestly.

Global attention gives you precise retrieval. If a token needs to look back ten thousand positions and copy something exactly, softmax attention does that almost for free, because the KV cache is a lossless record of everything you've seen. Linear attention, or any state-space style layer, compresses history into a fixed-size state. That compression is the whole point, since it's what gives you constant memory and linear time in sequence length, but it also means you're lossy by construction. You can make the state bigger, you can make the update rule smarter with gating or delta-rule style corrections, and that helps a lot, but you can't make a fixed-size state recall arbitrary details from arbitrarily long contexts. There's a hard information-theoretic ceiling there.

So when I design a hybrid, I'm asking: how few global layers can I get away with while still covering the retrieval-heavy behaviors, and can the linear layers handle everything else? In practice, "everything else" turns out to be most of the work. A lot of what a transformer does in its middle layers is local pattern mixing, in-context statistics, shaping representations. Linear layers are quite good at that, and they're much cheaper at long context. The things that break without global attention are needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, exact copying, multi-hop lookups where you need to chain several precise references together. A small number of full-attention layers, often something like one in six or one in eight, restores most of that.

The second part of the trade-off is where you put them and what the linear layers are doing around them. My intuition is that the linear layers should do the heavy lifting of building good representations so that when the attention layer fires, the queries and keys are already well-formed. If you put attention too early, it's working on raw embeddings and wastes capacity. If you put it only at the very end, the middle of the network has no way to retrieve. Interleaving, with the first global layer a few blocks in, tends to work best in my experience, though I'll be honest that a lot of this is still empirical rather than principled.

There's also a systems angle people underestimate. Even a small fraction of global attention means you still have a KV cache that grows with sequence length, so you don't get the pure constant-memory inference that a fully recurrent model promises. You've traded away the clean asymptotics. But a cache that's one-eighth the size is a genuinely different regime for serving, so I think of it as a very good deal rather than a compromise.

And the last thing I'd say is that the better the linear layers get, the fewer attention layers you need. That's really what drives my own research: improving the expressivity of the recurrent update so the fixed state is used more efficiently. Every improvement there shifts the balance point in the hybrid. So the trade-off isn't static. It's a moving target that depends on how good your linear primitive is, and I expect it to keep moving in the linear direction.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is where you actually need global attention. It gives you a direct way to retrieve information from anywhere in the context, but that becomes expensive as the sequence gets longer. Linear-attention layers can process long sequences more efficiently, but they typically compress the past into a fixed-size state, so some information can be lost.

In a hybrid architecture, you can use linear layers for much of the processing and keep global-attention layers where access to individual tokens is especially valuable. But the ratio isn’t the only thing that matters. Where you place those layers, and how well the two types work together during training, also matter.

So I would treat it as an empirical design problem: for a given latency and memory budget, how much global attention do you need to preserve the capabilities you care about? You want to measure both quality and actual serving performance, because a theoretically cheaper architecture doesn’t necessarily run faster on your hardware.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: where do you actually need global attention? Global attention gives you a very flexible way to retrieve information from the context, but its cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Linear attention can process long sequences more efficiently, but it compresses the history into a fixed-size state, so you’re making a trade-off in how much information you preserve and how precisely you can retrieve it.

In a hybrid, you can use linear layers for much of the processing and keep some global-attention layers for the interactions that benefit from that more precise retrieval. But the ratio and placement should be empirical questions. You want to evaluate not just language-modeling loss, but also retrieval tasks, different context lengths, and actual inference performance.

And the hardware matters. A theoretically cheaper layer isn’t necessarily faster at the sequence lengths and batch sizes you care about. So I’d think of it as a joint design problem: model quality, memory usage, and latency, rather than choosing a ratio based only on FLOPs.
